name: Turkish
sources: Zimmer, Karl & Orgun, Orhan (1999). Turkish. Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press.
Göksel, Aslı & Kerslake, Celia (2005). Turkish: A Comprehensive Grammar. Routledge.
Öğüt, Fatih; Kılıç, Mehmet Akif; Engin, Erkan Zeki & Midilli, Rasim (2006). Voice onset times for Turkish stop consonants. Speech Communication 48(9), 1094-1099.
Malkoç, Ekrem (2009). Türkçe ünlü formant frekans değerleri ve bu değerlere dayalı ünlü dörtgeni. Dil Dergisi 146, 71-85.
Kılıç, Mehmet Akif & Öğüt, Fatih (2004). A high unrounded vowel in Turkish: is it a central or back vowel? Speech Communication 43.
Levi, Susannah V. (2005). Acoustic correlates of lexical accent in Turkish. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 35(1), 73-97.
Sezer, Engin (1981). On non-final stress in Turkish. Journal of Turkish Studies 5.
Kabak, Barış & Vogel, Irene (2001). The phonological word and stress assignment in Turkish. Phonology 18(3).
Ipek, Canan & Jun, Sun-Ah (2013). Towards a model of intonational phonology of Turkish: neutral intonation. Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics 19.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (mean of 10 speakers, vowels in read CV and VC syllables)

contrasts: eight vowel qualities built on three binary oppositions: high versus non-high, front versus back, rounded versus unrounded (i y ɯ u, e ø a o)
voiced versus voiceless aspirated stops and affricates
palatal versus velar stops (c ɟ versus k ɡ) and clear versus dark laterals (l versus ɫ), contrastive only next to back vowels in loanwords (kâr versus kar, hâlâ versus hala)
vowel length, marginal: long vowels in Arabic and Persian loanwords and from lost ğ (dağ)
allophony: /k ɡ/ are palatal [c ɟ] and /l/ is clear [l] next to front vowels; [k ɡ ɫ] next to back vowels
voiceless stops and /tʃ/ are aspirated before vowels, weakly or not at all before consonants
/e/ lowers to [ɛ ~ æ] before a coda sonorant /m n l ɾ/ (gel [ɟæl], ben [bæn])
/i y u e ø/ are lowered to [ɪ ʏ ʊ ɛ œ] in a final open syllable of a phrase (Zimmer & Orgun 1999)
/ɾ/ is a tap in all positions; word-finally it is devoiced and fricated
/v/ weakens to an approximant [ʋ ~ w] between vowels and next to rounded vowels (tavuk)

ğ (yumuşak g, soft g) has no consonantal sound in the standard language: after a vowel in coda position it lengthens that vowel (dağ [daː], yağmur [jaːmuɾ]), between back vowels it is hiatus or a long vowel (ağaç [a.atʃ]), between front vowels a weak palatal glide (değil [dejil ~ deːil], iğne [iːne])
/h/ is weakened or lost between vowels and before consonants in casual speech, with lengthening of the vowel
word-final /b d dʒ ɡ/ are devoiced, shown in the spelling (kitap, kitabı)
high vowels may be devoiced or dropped between voiceless consonants in unstressed syllables in fast speech
/a/ is fronted [a] after palatal /c ɟ l/ in loans written with a circumflex (kâğıt, lâle)
phonotactics: no onset clusters in native words; loan clusters are usually broken by a high vowel (spor [sɯpoɾ]) or preceded by one (istasyon)
coda clusters are sonorant + obstruent or voiceless fricative + stop (Türk, genç, üst, çift)
backness harmony holds in native roots and in nearly all suffixes; rounding harmony applies to high suffix vowels only
/o ø/ occur almost only in the first syllable of native words
many loanwords and a few suffixes (-yor, -ken, -ki, -leyin, -gil) do not harmonise
ğ never begins a word; /ʒ/ occurs only in loans

stress.type: fixed final by default with lexical and morphological exceptions; realised as a pitch accent
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word including stressable suffixes; place names and many loans follow the Sezer pattern (antepenult if it is heavy and the penult is light, otherwise penult: Ánkara, İstánbul, lokánta), and pre-stressing suffixes and clitics (negative -mA, question mI, copular -(y)DI and -DIr, -(y)lA, -CA, -(y)ken, dA, ki) put the stress on the syllable before them.
stress.cues: mainly F0 (high pitch on the accented syllable), some intensity; little or no lengthening of the accented vowel (Levi 2005)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none: unstressed vowels keep their quality; only optional devoicing or loss of high vowels between voiceless consonants
rhythm.notes: Simple syllable structure and no vowel reduction; traditionally grouped with the syllable-timed languages.

length.notes: Long vowels are restricted to loanwords (sometimes marked by a circumflex, often unmarked: memur [meːmuɾ], şair [ʃaːiɾ]) and to compensatory lengthening from ğ and lost h. Geminates arise in loans and at morpheme boundaries. No reliable published duration ratio is given here.

intonation.declarative: prenuclear words or phrases rise to a high at their right edge; the nuclear accent is on the constituent just before the verb; everything after the nucleus is low and compressed; final low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: the particle mI follows the questioned constituent; high pitch on the syllable just before mI, then a fall to low; no final rise is required
intonation.wh_question: high peak on the wh-word followed by a fall to low, compressed pitch; a final rise is optional
intonation.continuation: high boundary (rise) at the end of a non-final phrase or clause
intonation.accent_shape: finally stressed words rise to a high on the last syllable (L ... H); words with non-final stress have a high on the stressed syllable followed by a fall (H*L)
intonation.notes: After Göksel & Kerslake 2005 and Ipek & Jun 2013.

tone.notes: Word accent is cued mostly by pitch (Levi 2005) but there is no lexical tone.

phonation: optional devoicing of high vowels between voiceless consonants

problems: p t k come from the base2 table and use unaspirated samples; Turkish voiceless stops are aspirated (VOT about 40-70 ms)
long vowels of loanwords are not produced: â î û are mapped to plain short a i u (hâlâ gives [hala]) and unmarked long vowels (memur, şair) have no dictionary entries
k is not palatalised before â (kâr gives [kar], expected [caɾ]) and has no palatal allophone rule before front vowels, although g becomes [ɟ] there; only the burst sample changes before i
non-final stress is only known for the roughly 150 entries of tr_listx (mostly place names): gazete, lokanta, şimdi, sonra, ancak get final stress
/ɾ/ is a trill except between vowels; the literature describes a tap everywhere, devoiced word-finally
lowering of i y u e ø to [ɪ ʏ ʊ ɛ œ] is applied in the last syllable of every word and before consonant clusters, wider than the phrase-final open syllable context described by Zimmer & Orgun
the ɯ target (F1 448, F2 1280 Hz) is lower and further back than measured values (about 400 and 1500 Hz)
no weakening of /v/ to [ʋ] and no loss of intervocalic /h/
good: soft g is handled as vowel lengthening, hiatus or [j] by context
final stress with the pre-stressing suffixes marked as unstressed in tr_rules (gelmedi, geliyor)
e-lowering before coda sonorants, clear and dark l, palatal ɟ
all eight vowel qualities present with formant targets close to published values; vowel harmony follows from the spelling

notes: Zimmer & Orgun list /ɣ/ for ğ as a phoneme without consonantal realisation; it is left out of the consonant list here and described under allophony.
